title: When a Private School Is 100% Publicly Funded
hook: Some private schools get every dollar of their tuition from taxpayers — yet the conflict-of-interest, open-records, and open-meeting rules that come with public money don't follow it in.
key_points: A '100% school' is a private school where taxpayer vouchers cover tuition for every enrolled student — publicly funded in practice, privately governed in law.
Wisconsin had 39 such schools in the most recent school year, enrolling 7,923 students on about $87 million in state voucher funding.
Unlike public schools, they need not serve students with disabilities, open their board meetings, or release contracts and financial records on request.
At Milwaukee's Atlas Preparatory — $4.3 million for 357 students, rated one star out of five — two of three board members were on the school's payroll.
The board chair drew $132,505 in salary plus benefits and his accounting firm held an $87,250 contract; the executive director earned $175,000 while sitting on the board.
Arrangements like these would breach conflict-of-interest rules at a public school, but Wisconsin places no such restriction on private voucher schools.
content_html: Public money usually arrives with strings: open meetings, records you can request, rules against paying yourself out of both pockets. ProPublica's Megan O'Matz went looking for what happens when those dollars land somewhere the strings don't reach — private schools where vouchers cover the tuition of every single student.
extra_html: Wisconsin had 39 of these "100% schools" in the most recent school year, enrolling 7,923 students on roughly $87 million in state voucher funding. They are, as the reporting puts it, funded like public schools but not operated with the same oversight or transparency: they need not serve students with disabilities, need not open board meetings to the public, and need not hand over contracts or financial documents on request. Milwaukee's Atlas Preparatory illustrates the consequence. The school took $4.3 million for 357 students while carrying the state's lowest performance rating — one star out of five, "fails to meet expectations." Two of its three board members were on its payroll: chair Steven Menden drew $132,505 in salary plus $19,916 in benefits and his accounting firm held an $87,250 contract, while executive director Michelle Lukacs earned $175,000 and also sat on the board. None of that violates Wisconsin law, because the conflict-of-interest rules that would forbid it apply to public schools. The general lesson travels beyond one state: accountability requirements in the U.S. typically attach to what kind of institution you are, not to where your funding came from — so routing public money through private entities can quietly move it outside the oversight built for it. (Voucher rules vary widely by state; the specifics here are Wisconsin's.)

related.title: Public Money, Private Oversight: The Voucher Accountability Gap
related.hook: Public schools face extensive state regulation. Private schools funded by the same taxpayer dollars, through vouchers, often don't — a gap one Arkansas case exposed starkly.

related.title: Accountability & Oversight
related.hook: Power left unwatched drifts toward abuse. Accountability is the demand that officials answer for what they do — and oversight is the machinery that makes them.

related.title: Freedom of Information
related.hook: You can't hold power to account for what you can't see. Freedom of information laws pry open the workings of government so citizens can actually check it.

flashcards.prompt: What is a '100% school' in the context of voucher programs?
flashcards.back_html: A private school where taxpayer-funded vouchers cover tuition for every enrolled student — funded like a public school, but governed under private-school rules.

flashcards.prompt: Which obligation applies to Wisconsin public schools but not to the private schools taking their voucher money?

choices.text: Opening board meetings to the public and releasing contracts on request
Reporting standardized test scores, which Wisconsin voucher schools are exempt from
Employing licensed staff, which no school in the state is required to do

flashcards.explanation_html: Wisconsin is one of the states that does require voucher schools to report test scores. What doesn't carry over is the transparency layer: open meetings, open records, and serving students with disabilities.

flashcards.prompt: What did ProPublica find about Atlas Preparatory's board?

choices.text: Two of its three members were on the school's payroll
It had no members, leaving the school ungoverned
Its members were appointed directly by the state education agency
It voted to return its voucher funding after a poor performance rating

flashcards.explanation_html: The board chair drew a salary and held a separate contract through his accounting firm; the executive director sat on the board she reported to. A public school could not staff its board this way.

flashcards.prompt: Why does the 'quasi-public' label matter for accountability, rather than being a technicality?
flashcards.back_html: Accountability rules in the U.S. generally attach to the type of institution, not the source of its money. So when public dollars flow into a private entity, the oversight that normally rides along with them does not.
